title: Τέττιξ καὶ ἀλώπηξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 335. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τέττιξ ἐπί τινος ὑψηλοῦ δένδρου ᾖδεν.
sentences.tr: Tettix epi tinos hypsēlou dendrou ēiden.
sentences.l: A cicada was singing on a certain high tree.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ βουλομένη αὐτὸν καταφαγεῖν τοιοῦτόν τι ἐπενόησεν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de boulomenē auton kataphagein toiouton ti epenoēsen.
sentences.l: And a fox, wishing to devour him, contrived something of this sort.

sentences.t: Ἄντικρυς στᾶσα ἐθαύμαζεν αὐτοῦ τὴν εὐφωνίαν, καὶ παρεκάλει καταβῆναι, λέγουσα ὅτι ἐπιθυμεῖ θεάσασθαι πηλίκον ζῷον τηλικαύτην φωνὴν φθέγγεται.
sentences.tr: Antikrys stasa ethaumazen autou tēn euphōnian, kai parekalei katabēnai, legousa hoti epithymei theasasthai pēlikon zōion tēlikautēn phōnēn phthengetai.
sentences.l: Having taken her stand straight in front of him, she was marvelling at his fine voice, and kept urging him to come down, saying that she desires to behold how great a creature it is that utters so great a sound.
sentences.i: Taking her stand right in front of him, she marvelled at his fine voice and kept begging him to come down, saying that she longed to see how big a creature it was that produced so great a sound.
sentences.n: πηλίκον … τηλικαύτην are a correlative pair, 'how great' answered by 'so great', and πηλίκον ζῷον opens an indirect question depending on θεάσασθαι. The present ἐπιθυμεῖ is kept after the past παρεκάλει: Greek leaves the tense of the original words standing where English shifts it back to 'longed'.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος ὑπονοήσας αὐτῆς τὴν ἐνέδραν, φύλλον ἀποσπάσας καθῆκε.
sentences.tr: Kakeinos hyponoēsas autēs tēn enedran, phyllon apospasas kathēke.
sentences.l: And he, suspecting her ambush, having plucked off a leaf, let it fall.
sentences.i: And he, suspecting her trap, plucked off a leaf and let it drop.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is καὶ ἐκεῖνος run together by crasis. The two aorist participles hung on a single main verb are the fable's ordinary engine: everything preparatory goes into participles and the finite verb carries only the decisive act.

sentences.t: Προσδραμούσης δὲ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸν τέττιγα, ἔφη· « Ἀλλὰ πεπλάνησαι, ὦ αὕτη, εἰ ὑπέλαβές με καταβήσεσθαι· ἐγὼ γὰρ ἀπ’ ἐκείνου ἀλώπεκας φυλάττομαι ἀφ’ οὗ ἐν ἀφοδεύματι ἀλώπεκος πτερὰ τέττιγος ἐθεασάμην. »
sentences.tr: Prosdramousēs de hōs epi ton tettiga, ephē· « Alla peplanēsai, ō hautē, ei hypelabes me katabēsesthai· egō gar ap’ ekeinou alōpekas phylattomai aph’ hou en aphodeumati alōpekos ptera tettigos etheasamēn. »
sentences.l: And she having run forward as though at the cicada, he said: « But you are deceived, you there, if you supposed that I would come down; for I guard myself against foxes from that day from which I beheld a cicada's wings in a fox's droppings. »
sentences.i: And when she ran forward as though at the cicada, he said: « You are mistaken, you there, if you supposed I would come down; for I have been wary of foxes ever since the day I saw a cicada's wings in a fox's droppings. »
sentences.n: The genitive absolute προσδραμούσης has no expressed subject — the fox is left to be understood from what precedes, which Greek allows freely. ὡς ἐπί marks the movement as made on an assumption, 'as if for' the cicada. ὦ αὕτη is a brusque form of address, the nominative used for the vocative, roughly 'you there'. ἀπ’ ἐκείνου … ἀφ’ οὗ is a correlative pair, 'from that time … from which', where English says 'ever since'.

sentences.t: Ὅτι τοὺς φρονίμους τῶν ἀνθρώπων αἱ τῶν πέλας συμφοραὶ σωφρονίζουσι.
sentences.tr: Hoti tous phronimous tōn anthrōpōn hai tōn pelas symphorai sōphronizousi.
sentences.l: That the prudent among men, the misfortunes of those near them bring to their senses.
sentences.i: The story shows that the misfortunes of their neighbours bring the prudent among men to their senses.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. The object stands first, as in the Greek, so that the subject arrives last. πέλας is an adverb, 'near by', and takes the article to make a noun of it, 'those close at hand'. σωφρονίζω is to make a person σώφρων — to teach him sense, whether by warning or by chastisement.
